title: Parity-dependent coupling of molecular spin chains to a superconductor
authors: Katerina Vaxevani, Jon Ortuzar, Stefano Trivini, Georg Monninger, Dongfei Wang, Vilas-Varela, Lucía Gómez-Rodrigo, Diego Peña, Jose Ignacio Pascual
abstract: Topological order can fractionalize the quantum numbers of the underlying particles. A paradigmatic example is the spin-1/2 states at the edges of an antiferromagnetic integer-spin chain, protected by a topological Haldane gap in the bulk and mutually coupled in short chains. Owing to their topological protection, they are natural building blocks for hybrid spin-superconductor quantum systems. Whether fractionalization survives the coupling to a superconducting condensate, however, remains an open question. Here we grow molecular Haldane chains of antiferromagnetically coupled spin-1 triangulene units on a proximitized Au(111)/Nb(110) surface and resolve a parity-dependent coupling of their spin-1/2 edge states to the superconducting condensate by scanning tunnelling spectroscopy. Odd-length chains host Yu-Shiba-Rusinov bound states inside the superconducting gap, originating from the net S=1 ground state, whereas even-length chains form an S=0 ground state decoupled from the superconductor. A two-site superconductor model reveals that this alternation arises from the sign and strength of the inter-edge interaction, a mechanism independently validated by extra-gap spin excitations in tunnelling spectra. Collective many-body spin excitation modes are also detected decoupled from the superconductor by the much larger Haldane gap. The length-tunable coupling of the edge spins to the superconductor opens a route toward molecular spin qubits based on $π$-conjugated carbon architectures.
summary: This paper reports on the parity-dependent coupling between molecular spin chains and a superconductor using STS on triangulene chains. They found that odd-length chains exhibit superconducting gap features (YSR states) due to their net S=1 ground state, while even-length chains are decoupled. This demonstrates a controllable mechanism for engineering spin-superconductor hybrid quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates whether the topological fractionalization of quantum numbers in molecular spin chains survives when coupled to a superconducting condensate.
main_result: The coupling exhibits a parity dependence: odd-length chains host Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states from an S=1 ground state, while even-length chains form an S=0 ground state decoupled from the superconductor.
method: The research combines scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) measurements on molecular chains with theoretical modeling using spin Hamiltonians.
model_or_system: The system consists of molecular Haldane chains of spin-1 triangulene units grown on a proximitized Au(111)/Nb(110) superconducting surface. The physics is modeled using effective spin Hamiltonians incorporating inter-edge interactions and superconducting coupling.
key_observables: Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound states inside the superconducting gap, and extra-gap singlet-triplet (ST) excitations.
important_parameters: Chain length parity (odd vs. even), superconducting gap ($\Delta$), and the strength of inter-edge exchange interactions ($J$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the superconducting gap is protected by the quasiparticle gap, and the mechanism is governed by the sign and strength of inter-edge interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system setup, STM topography, and dI/dV spectra comparing even and odd chains, showing the characteristic alternation of YSR resonances versus ST peaks.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical system and the open question, presenting STS measurements showing parity dependence, developing theoretical models (e.g., two-site superconductor model), and concluding with the implications for molecular spin qubits.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the interplay between topological quantum states (Haldane chains) and superconducting proximity effects, which is central to building solid-state quantum devices and understanding emergent superconducting phenomena in molecular systems.
